query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Inserting a thin refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) interlayer (such as (CrFeTiTa)70W30) at the W–Cu interface of the composite will mitigate phase separation and suppress interfacial void formation during thermal cycling and irradiation, thereby improving the composite’s thermal conductivity relative to an untreated composite.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite with either discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix that suffers from phase separation and interfacial void formation under service conditions.
generation.intervention: Deposit or incorporate a thin RHEA interlayer between the W and Cu phases.
generation.conditions: Processing and service conditions typical of plasma–facing material joints and cooling components; specifically, exposure to heat-transfer environments (with temperatures ranging up to approximately 1100–1500 °C) and high-fluence ion irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: The RHEA interlayer provides a graded structural bond at the W–Cu interface, reducing thermal expansion mismatch and acting as a diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: The RHEA interlayer minimizes interdiffusion between W and Cu by offering chemical and structural compatibility, which suppresses the nucleation of voids and impedes phase separation. This maintains a more coherent interface that preserves thermal conductivity even under thermal cycling and irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The composite with the RHEA interlayer will demonstrate improved interfacial integrity and, as a result, higher thermal conductivity compared to the untreated composite when subjected to similar heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: An untreated W–Cu composite that, under similar thermal and irradiation conditions, shows detrimental phase separation and interfacial void formation, leading to reduced thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective within the high temperature (up to ~1500 °C) and high-fluence irradiation environments relevant to plasma-facing component joints, though the optimal RHEA layer thickness and exact composition need further refinement.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in thermal conductivity and the optimal processing parameters for the RHEA interlayer remain to be determined. Uncertainties include the interlayer’s long‐term stability under cyclic thermal and irradiation stresses and its compatibility with existing manufacturing processes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set incorporating the thin RHEA interlayer at the interface and a control set without the interlayer. Subject both sets to accelerated thermal cycling (e.g., exposure to temperatures up to 1500 °C) and ion irradiation mimicking fusion-relevant fluences. Post-treatment, characterize the interfacial microstructure (using electron microscopy and spectroscopy) and measure thermal conductivity.
measurements: Interfacial microstructure imaging to assess phase separation and void formation
Thermal conductivity measurements before and after treatment
Irradiation damage quantification using ion-beam analysis techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RHEA-interlayered samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in phase separation and interfacial voids or do not maintain higher thermal conductivity compared to the untreated controls under the same thermal and irradiation conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractNuclear fusion is a promising energy source. The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed.
